claim: Native cargo proteins exit the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COPII-coated vesicles.
source: Native cargo proteins exit the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COPII-coated vesicles, whereas resident and misfolded proteins are substantially excluded from vesicles by a retention mechanism that remains unresolved.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by the broader scientific literature.

claim: Resident and misfolded proteins are substantially excluded from COPII vesicles by a retention mechanism.
source: Native cargo proteins exit the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COPII-coated vesicles, whereas resident and misfolded proteins are substantially excluded from vesicles by a retention mechanism that remains unresolved.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field, though the mechanism is noted as unresolved.

claim: The ER retention mechanism remains unresolved.
source: Native cargo proteins exit the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in COPII-coated vesicles, whereas resident and misfolded proteins are substantially excluded from vesicles by a retention mechanism that remains unresolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: 4-PBA targets COPII protein to reduce the stringency of retention.
source: We probed the ER retention process using the proteostasis regulator 4-phenylbutyrate (4-PBA), which we show targets COPII protein to reduce the stringency of retention.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by crystallographic and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 4-PBA competes with p24 proteins to bind COPII.
source: 4-PBA competes with p24 proteins to bind COPII.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data showing 4-PBA binding to the B site of Sec24 and by vesicle budding experiments showing reduced p24 packaging in the presence of 4-PBA.

claim: When p24 protein uptake is blocked, COPII vesicles package resident proteins.
source: When p24 protein uptake is blocked, COPII vesicles package resident proteins and an ER-trapped mutant LDL receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by budding experiments using B-site mutant COPII protein and 4-PBA treatment, shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: When p24 protein uptake is blocked, COPII vesicles package an ER-trapped mutant LDL receptor.
source: When p24 protein uptake is blocked, COPII vesicles package resident proteins and an ER-trapped mutant LDL receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by budding experiments showing increased packaging of G544V-mutant LDL receptor with B-site mutant COPII and 4-PBA treatment (Figure 3).

claim: 4-PBA triggers the secretion of a KDEL-tagged luminal resident.
source: We further show that 4-PBA triggers the secretion of a KDEL-tagged luminal resident, implying that a compromised retention mechanism causes saturation of the KDEL retrieval system.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing dose-dependent secretion of GRP94 in response to 4-PBA treatment (Figure 5).

claim: A compromised retention mechanism causes saturation of the KDEL retrieval system.
source: We further show that 4-PBA triggers the secretion of a KDEL-tagged luminal resident, implying that a compromised retention mechanism causes saturation of the KDEL retrieval system.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 4-PBA causes secretion of KDEL-tagged GRP94, which would only occur if the KDEL retrieval system is saturated.

claim: Stringent ER retention requires the COPII coat machinery to actively sort biosynthetic cargo from diffusible misfolded and resident ER proteins.
source: The results indicate that stringent ER retention requires the COPII coat machinery to actively sort biosynthetic cargo from diffusible misfolded and resident ER proteins.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including crystallography, vesicle budding assays, and secretion experiments.

claim: Resident chaperones and bound folding intermediates make up the majority of ER content.
source: Resident chaperones and bound folding intermediates make up the majority of ER content and must be retained at that site (Barlowe and Helenius, 2016; Gomez-Navarro and Miller, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Resident proteins must be retained in the ER.
source: Resident chaperones and bound folding intermediates make up the majority of ER content and must be retained at that site (Barlowe and Helenius, 2016; Gomez-Navarro and Miller, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Resident complexes diffuse relatively freely in the ER.
source: A simple model for retention would be for resident proteins to consolidate into immobile networks too large to enter COPII vesicles, but data indicate instead that resident complexes diffuse relatively freely in the ER (Hendershot, 2000; Nehls et al., 2000), leaving the mechanism of ER retention an open problem.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Residents can escape the ER and are selectively retrieved from post-ER compartments by the KDEL receptor.
source: It is known that residents can escape the ER and are selectively retrieved from post-ER compartments, in particular by the KDEL receptor; however, when the KDEL signal is removed from a resident chaperone, its exit is considerably slower than the bulk flow rate (Barlowe and Helenius, 2016; Munro and Pelham, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When the KDEL signal is removed from a resident chaperone, its exit is considerably slower than the bulk flow rate.
source: It is known that residents can escape the ER and are selectively retrieved from post-ER compartments, in particular by the KDEL receptor; however, when the KDEL signal is removed from a resident chaperone, its exit is considerably slower than the bulk flow rate (Barlowe and Helenius, 2016; Munro and Pelham, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: p24-family proteins cycle continuously between ER and Golgi membranes as abundant constituents of COPI and COPII vesicles.
source: These highly conserved transmembrane proteins cycle continuously between ER and Golgi membranes as abundant constituents of COPI and COPII vesicles (Kaiser, 2000; Otte et al., 2001; Stamnes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutation of p24 genes results in post-ER trafficking of a misfolded protein in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Mutation of p24 genes results in post-ER trafficking of a misfolded protein in Caenorhabditis elegans (Wen and Greenwald, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of p24 genes in yeast causes misfolded proteins and chaperones to escape the ER.
source: Also, deletion of p24 genes in yeast causes misfolded proteins and chaperones to escape the ER, with the latter being secreted into the extracellular medium; however, these effects may be attributable in part to a chronic unfolded protein response (UPR) in the knockout strains (Belden and Barlowe, 2001; Copic et al., 2009; Elrod-Erickson and Kaiser, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The effects of p24 deletion in yeast may be attributable in part to a chronic unfolded protein response (UPR) in the knockout strains.
source: Also, deletion of p24 genes in yeast causes misfolded proteins and chaperones to escape the ER, with the latter being secreted into the extracellular medium; however, these effects may be attributable in part to a chronic unfolded protein response (UPR) in the knockout strains (Belden and Barlowe, 2001; Copic et al., 2009; Elrod-Erickson and Kaiser, 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of prior findings, supported by citations.

claim: 4-phenylbutyrate restores trafficking of various misfolded, ER-trapped mutant proteins expressed in cultured cells.
source: In a distinct line of research, the small molecule 4-phenylbutyrate has been shown to restore trafficking of various misfolded, ER-trapped mutant proteins expressed in cultured cells, including for example the △F508 mutant cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (Liu et al., 2004; Rubenstein et al., 1997; Zode et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 4-PBA reduces ER stress and attenuates the UPR.
source: Generally, 4-PBA also reduces ER stress and attenuates the UPR in these systems.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: The target and mechanism of action of 4-PBA are unknown.
source: The target and mechanism of action of 4-PBA are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: 4-PBA has a structural formula that resembles the cytoplasmic ER export signal of p24 proteins.
source: Notably, 4-PBA has a structural formula that resembles the cytoplasmic ER export signal of p24 proteins—one or two C-terminal hydrophobic residues, termed the ΦC motif (Nakamura et al., 1998; Nufer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an observation about structural similarity, with citations to prior work on the ΦC motif.

claim: The ΦC motif comprises one or two C-terminal hydrophobic residues.
source: Notably, 4-PBA has a structural formula that resembles the cytoplasmic ER export signal of p24 proteins—one or two C-terminal hydrophobic residues, termed the ΦC motif (Nakamura et al., 1998; Nufer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The packaging of cargo transmembrane proteins into COPII-coated vesicles entails a direct interaction between COPII protein and cytoplasmically-oriented ER export signals.
source: The packaging of cargo transmembrane proteins into COPII-coated vesicles entails a direct interaction between COPII protein and cytoplasmically-oriented ER export signals.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: About a half dozen export signals have been identified to date.
source: About a half dozen export signals have been identified to date, almost all comprising short peptide motifs, all of them binding to the Sec24 subunit of the COPII inner coat (Gomez-Navarro and Miller, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Almost all export signals comprise short peptide motifs.
source: About a half dozen export signals have been identified to date, almost all comprising short peptide motifs, all of them binding to the Sec24 subunit of the COPII inner coat (Gomez-Navarro and Miller, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All export signals bind to the Sec24 subunit of the COPII inner coat.
source: About a half dozen export signals have been identified to date, almost all comprising short peptide motifs, all of them binding to the Sec24 subunit of the COPII inner coat (Gomez-Navarro and Miller, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The ΦC export signal comprises a C-terminal signature of a pair of hydrophobic residues or a single terminal valine residue.
source: The ΦC export signal was identified in studies of p24-family and ERGIC-53 proteins, and comprises a C-terminal signature of a pair of hydrophobic residues or a single terminal valine residue (Nakamura et al., 1998; Nufer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The binding site of the ΦC motif on the COPII coat has been difficult to identify biochemically.
source: Despite clear evidence for the ΦC motif as a signal for ER export, its binding site on the COPII coat has been difficult to identify biochemically.
evidence: This is a statement about prior challenges in the field.

claim: Residual electron density matching ΦC peptide sequences is observed in Sec23a/Sec24a•Sec22b crystals soaked with ΦC peptides.
source: For all ΦC sequences, we observed clear evidence for peptide binding to a site on Sec24a in the Sec23a/Sec24a•Sec22b crystals, based on the presence of residual electron density that matches the peptide sequence
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1 and Table 1.

claim: ΦC peptides bind to a site on Sec24a.
source: For all ΦC sequences, we observed clear evidence for peptide binding to a site on Sec24a in the Sec23a/Sec24a•Sec22b crystals, based on the presence of residual electron density that matches the peptide sequence
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ΦC motif contacts the B site on Sec24a.
source: The ΦC motif contacts a site on Sec24a that is also the binding site for the LxxLE- and DxE-class export motifs (Miller et al., 2003; Mossessova et al., 2003; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and citations to prior work.

claim: The B site is the binding site for the LxxLE- and DxE-class export motifs.
source: The ΦC motif contacts a site on Sec24a that is also the binding site for the LxxLE- and DxE-class export motifs (Miller et al., 2003; Mossessova et al., 2003; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutation of B site residues impairs packaging of p24 proteins into COPII vesicles budded from yeast microsomal membranes.
source: Referred to as the B site, this was identified previously as a potential binding site for p24 proteins, as mutation of residues therein impairs packaging of p24 proteins into COPII vesicles budded from yeast microsomal membranes; however, the conclusion was a tentative one since residual p24 packaging was observed (Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Multiple classes of export motifs bind to a common site on Sec24.
source: The finding that multiple classes of export motifs bind to a common site is surprising, but the COPII•ΦC crystal structures highlight that the common molecular feature is carboxylate-group recognition by the clustered arginine residues of the B site
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The common molecular feature of export motif binding is carboxylate-group recognition by the clustered arginine residues of the B site.
source: The finding that multiple classes of export motifs bind to a common site is surprising, but the COPII•ΦC crystal structures highlight that the common molecular feature is carboxylate-group recognition by the clustered arginine residues of the B site
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and structural analysis.

claim: The terminal carboxylate group of the ΦC motif adopts a similar position and bonding arrangement to the carboxylate of the glutamate side chains of LxxLE and DxE motifs.
source: the terminal carboxylate group of the ΦC motif adopts a similar position and bonding arrangement to the carboxylate of the glutamate side chains of LxxLE and DxE motifs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Mancias and Goldberg, 2008; Mossessova et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data and citations to prior structures.

claim: Specific recognition of the ΦC motif involves the terminal carboxylate group bonding to Arg750 and Arg752 of Sec24a.
source: Thus, specific recognition of the ΦC motif involves the terminal carboxylate group bonding to Arg750 and Arg752 of Sec24a, with the penultimate hydrophobic residue of the motif nestling against Tyr496, and the terminal hydrophobic residue fitting to a pocket of hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1B–E and S1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The penultimate hydrophobic residue of the ΦC motif nestles against Tyr496.
source: Thus, specific recognition of the ΦC motif involves the terminal carboxylate group bonding to Arg750 and Arg752 of Sec24a, with the penultimate hydrophobic residue of the motif nestling against Tyr496, and the terminal hydrophobic residue fitting to a pocket of hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1B–E and S1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The terminal hydrophobic residue of the ΦC motif fits to a pocket of hydrophobic side chains.
source: Thus, specific recognition of the ΦC motif involves the terminal carboxylate group bonding to Arg750 and Arg752 of Sec24a, with the penultimate hydrophobic residue of the motif nestling against Tyr496, and the terminal hydrophobic residue fitting to a pocket of hydrophobic side chains (Figure 1B–E and S1).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A terminal valine is the most favored residue in the ΦC motif because its fit to the pocket allows optimal geometry for bonding to the terminal carboxylate group.
source: Evidently, the B-site hydrophobic pocket accommodates a range of hydrophobic side chains; however, a terminal valine is the most favored residue because its fit to the pocket allows optimal geometry for bonding to the terminal carboxylate group (shown schematically in Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from crystallographic data and is consistent with functional data from prior literature.

claim: 4-PBA binds to the B site of Sec24a.
source: Difference Fourier maps calculated from X-ray diffraction data show clear evidence for binding of 4-PBA to the B site of Sec24a (Figure 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 1F-I.

claim: 4-PBA closely mimics the terminal phenylalanine side chain and carboxylate group of the Phe-Phe motif of ERGIC-53.
source: 4-PBA closely mimics the terminal phenylalanine side chain and carboxylate group of the Phe-Phe motif of ERGIC-53 (compare Figure 1E and I).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data comparing the binding modes in Figure 1E and 1I.

claim: The residues contacting 4-PBA are almost invariant among the four human Sec24 paralogs.
source: The residues contacting 4-PBA are almost invariant among the four human Sec24 paralogs; only Sec24a residue I818 (drawn in Figure 1I) varies, and the change is a conservative one to leucine in Sec24c/d.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison and structural analysis.

claim: 4-PBA binds the COPII coat at relevant concentrations.
source: In summary, the crystallographic result gives evidence that 4-PBA binds the COPII coat at relevant concentrations of the small molecule.
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data showing binding at 1-50 mM concentrations.

claim: The L750W mutation in Sec24d blocks binding of all ligands to the B site.
source: We have modeled the Sec24d-L750W mutation in Figure 2B to indicate that the tryptophan side chain is restricted to a single rotamer, and this conformation is predicted to block binding of all ligands to the B site.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Sec23/Sec24-L616W mutant protein lost all ability to package LxxLE- and DxE-signal cargoes in yeast.
source: This mutation was designed previously for a study of yeast COPII (Miller et al., 2003), where it was reported that the corresponding Sec23/Sec24-L616W mutant protein lost all ability to package LxxLE- and DxE-signal cargoes, and exhibited reduced packaging efficiency of Erp1p (a p24 protein) and Emp47p (yeast ERGIC-53 homolog); COPII-coated vesicles budded with the mutant protein exhibited negligible differences in size and morphology when compared to wild-type vesicles (Miller et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The uptake of p24 proteins and ERGIC-53 into vesicles by Sec23a/24d-L750W mutant COPII was substantially reduced to 5–8% of that obtained with wild-type COPII.
source: As seen in Figure 2A and C, the uptake of p24 proteins (p24α3 and p24β1) and ERGIC-53 into vesicles by Sec23a/24d-L750W mutant COPII was substantially reduced, to just 5–8% of that obtained with wild-type COPII.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and C.

claim: The total yield of COPII vesicles is significantly lower for the mutant coat.
source: However, the total yield of COPII vesicles is significantly lower for the mutant coat, which we infer is due to the decreased number of contacts made between coat protein and transmembrane cargo, a phenomenon reported previously for mammalian and yeast COPI-coated vesicles (Bremser et al., 1999; Sandmann et al., 2003).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data and explained by inference with support from citations to prior literature.

claim: Blockade of the B site in Sec24d-L750W reduced the packaging rate of p24α3 and p24β1 to 20–25% of the wild-type level.
source: Thus, blockade of the B site in Sec24d-L750W reduced the packaging rate of p24α3 and p24β1 to 20–25% of the wild-type level (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D after correction for budding yield.

claim: The residual p24 packaging in B-site-mutant COPII constitutes the bulk flow (passive) level of uptake.
source: This residual p24 packaging is at a similar level to that reported for yeast B-site-mutant COPII (Miller et al., 2003), and we infer that it constitutes the bulk flow (passive) level of uptake of these proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with prior literature.

claim: 10 mM 4-PBA causes a 50% reduction in the packaging rate of p24 proteins and ERGIC-53.
source: Significantly, when COPII vesicles were budded in the presence of 10 mM 4-PBA, we observed a 50% reduction in the packaging rate of p24 proteins and ERGIC-53 (Figure 2A and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and D.

claim: The EC50 of 4-PBA in a cell-based transport assay is 6.4 mM.
source: This concentration of 4-PBA is slightly above its EC50 of 6.4 mM as measured in a cell-based transport assay (see Figure 3B and below)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All four human paralogs of Sec24 package ERGIC-53.
source: Previously we showed that all four human paralogs of Sec24 package ERGIC-53 (Mancias and Goldberg, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: COPII vesicles package p24 proteins to high levels because all paralogs of Sec24 can bind the ΦC motif.
source: thus we surmise that COPII vesicles package p24 proteins to high levels (Otte et al., 2001) because all paralogs of Sec24 can bind the ΦC motif, and that all are targets of 4-PBA.
evidence: This is inferred from the crystallographic and functional data, with a citation supporting high-level packaging.

claim: All Sec24 paralogs are targets of 4-PBA.
source: thus we surmise that COPII vesicles package p24 proteins to high levels (Otte et al., 2001) because all paralogs of Sec24 can bind the ΦC motif, and that all are targets of 4-PBA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 4-PBA binds to Sec24a and Sec24d, and the residues are conserved.

claim: The G544V-mutant LDL receptor fails to reach the Golgi complex.
source: The G544V-mutant LDL receptor fails to reach the Golgi complex (Tveten et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and confirmed by data in Figure 3A.

claim: The G544V-mutant LDL receptor is not thermoreversible.
source: We verified that the mutant LDL receptor is not thermoreversible, since there was no evidence for transport to the Golgi complex during a 2 hr temperature shift of the cells to 30°C (Figure 3A; transport to the Golgi is monitored by the acquisition of Golgi-specific glycosylation to yield a 160 kDa form).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Application of 10 mM 4-PBA to cells restored the trafficking of as much as 25% of the G544V-mutant LDL receptor.
source: And we observed that application of 10 mM 4-PBA to cells restored the trafficking of as much as 25% of the receptor (Figure 3B), in line with the results reported in Tveten et al. (2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The depletion from vesicles of p24 proteins caused by 10 mM 4-PBA and by B-site mutation is accompanied by a significant enrichment of residents and mutant LDL receptor.
source: Remarkably, the depletion from vesicles of p24 proteins caused by 10 mM 4-PBA and by B-site mutation is accompanied by a significant enrichment of residents and mutant LDL receptor (Figure 3C; Figure 3D and E show the packaging rates corrected for change in budding yield).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII package five times as much calnexin as wild-type vesicles.
source: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII package five times as much calnexin as wild-type vesicles; the enrichment factors for BiP, GRP94 and mutant LDL receptor are all approximately 4-fold, and the protein disulfide isomerase ERp57 (PDIA3) is enriched 9-fold (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: BiP, GRP94 and mutant LDL receptor are enriched approximately 4-fold in vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII.
source: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII package five times as much calnexin as wild-type vesicles; the enrichment factors for BiP, GRP94 and mutant LDL receptor are all approximately 4-fold, and the protein disulfide isomerase ERp57 (PDIA3) is enriched 9-fold (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: ERp57 is enriched 9-fold in vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII.
source: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII package five times as much calnexin as wild-type vesicles; the enrichment factors for BiP, GRP94 and mutant LDL receptor are all approximately 4-fold, and the protein disulfide isomerase ERp57 (PDIA3) is enriched 9-fold (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Protein sorting by the COPII coat yields a 15- to 25-fold purification of p24 proteins from ER residents.
source: Thus, protein sorting by the COPII coat yields a 15- to 25-fold purification of p24 proteins from ER residents—purification here refers to the product of resident-protein depletion and p24 enrichment in wild-type vesicles relative to B-site-mutant vesicles.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 3D-E.

claim: Resident-protein complexes are sufficiently small to be packaged into mutant and 4-PBA-treated COPII vesicles.
source: A corollary of these observations is that resident-protein complexes are sufficiently small to be packaged into mutant and 4-PBA-treated COPII vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that resident proteins are packaged into vesicles when p24 sorting is disrupted.

claim: The reciprocal relationship between packaging of p24 proteins and residents is consistent with an active sorting mechanism involving p24-dependent exclusion of diffusible resident-protein complexes.
source: Thus, the reciprocal relationship that we observe between packaging of p24 proteins and residents is consistent with the model of an active sorting mechanism involving p24-dependent exclusion of diffusible resident-protein complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of reciprocal packaging rates.

claim: The expression of ER-trapped G544V-mutant LDL receptor in the CHO cell line induces ER stress and UPR activation.
source: Specifically, the expression of ER-trapped G544V-mutant LDL receptor in the CHO cell line has been shown to induce ER stress and UPR activation, such that downstream markers of stress, including ER chaperone levels, are maximally expressed at the time of cell harvesting for our budding experiments (Sørensen et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The deletion of p24 genes in yeast causes a chronic UPR.
source: An additional complication is that the deletion of p24 genes in yeast causes a chronic UPR (Belden and Barlowe, 2001), raising the possibility that the leakage phenotype of the yeast knockout is due entirely to UPR activation rather than a breakdown of the active sorting mechanism that we posit.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The packaging of proteins into vesicles budded from parent CHO cells exhibits the same pattern of p24-dependence as from stressed cells.
source: As shown in Figure 4, the packaging of proteins into vesicles budded from parent CHO cells exhibits the same pattern of p24-dependence as from stressed cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII from unstressed cells are depleted of p24 proteins by a factor of ~8 fold.
source: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII are depleted of p24 proteins by a factor of ~8 fold (Figure 4B), yet the same pool of vesicles packages on average 5.5-fold higher levels of resident proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII from unstressed cells package on average 5.5-fold higher levels of resident proteins.
source: Vesicles budded with B-site-mutant COPII are depleted of p24 proteins by a factor of ~8 fold (Figure 4B), yet the same pool of vesicles packages on average 5.5-fold higher levels of resident proteins (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The COPII coat achieves ~40 fold purification of p24 proteins from resident proteins in unstressed cells.
source: This indicates a ~40 fold purification achieved by the COPII coat, though we note that this calculation is rather inaccurate because the packaging of residents by wild-type COPII is close to background levels (Figure 4A and Table 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Wild-type COPII vesicles package resident proteins at a 5-fold higher rate from stressed cells than from unstressed cells.
source: Quantification of these data in Table 3 shows that wild-type COPII vesicles package resident proteins at a 5-fold higher rate from stressed cells than from unstressed cells, whereas the packaging rates of bona fide cargo proteins are essentially the same.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Table 3.

claim: The packaging rates of bona fide cargo proteins are essentially the same in stressed and unstressed cells.
source: Quantification of these data in Table 3 shows that wild-type COPII vesicles package resident proteins at a 5-fold higher rate from stressed cells than from unstressed cells, whereas the packaging rates of bona fide cargo proteins are essentially the same.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Table 3.

claim: 4-PBA causes secretion of GRP94 from stressed and unstressed cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Strikingly, we observed secretion of GRP94, dose-dependent on 4-PBA and maximal at 20 mM 4-PBA, from both stressed and unstressed cells (Figure 5A and B, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: GRP94 is released by secretion rather than by cell lysis.
source: GRP94 is released by secretion rather than by cell lysis, because the cytosolic marker GAPDH is absent from the extracellular sample.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: At 45 mM 4-PBA, cell lysis is detected and the cells have lost all ability to secrete GRP94.
source: At the highest concentration, 45 mM 4-PBA, cell lysis is detected and the cells have lost all ability to secrete GRP94.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The profile of GRP94 secretion from stressed CHO cells closely matches that of the restoration of trafficking of the mutant LDL receptor.
source: Thus, the profile of GRP94 secretion from stressed CHO cells closely matches that of the restoration of trafficking of the mutant LDL receptor (compare Figures 3B and 5A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data in Figures 3B and 5A.

claim: Stressed cells secrete GRP94 in the absence of 4-PBA.
source: First, stressed cells secrete GRP94 in the absence of 4-PBA (albeit at low levels), matching a prior observation of BiP secretion from yeast cells following UPR induction with β-mercaptoethanol (Belden and Barlowe, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is an apparent linear relationship between 4-PBA concentration and GRP94 secretion for stressed cells.
source: Second, there is an apparent linear relationship between 4-PBA concentration and GRP94 secretion for stressed cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Resident protein leakage into COPII vesicles in stressed cells delivers KDEL ligands to post-ER membranes at levels that approach or exceed the capacity of the retrieval system.
source: Since the KDEL retrieval system is known to be readily saturable (Dean and Pelham, 1990), these two observations indicate that resident protein leakage into COPII vesicles in stressed cells, even in the absence of 4-PBA, delivers KDEL ligands to post-ER membranes at levels that approach or exceed the capacity of the retrieval system.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and supported by a citation about KDEL system saturability.

claim: The profile of GRP94 secretion from unstressed cells is a step response.
source: Third, the profile of GRP94 secretion from unstressed cells is a step response; only at high concentrations of 4-PBA does resident leakage seem to exceed a threshold level to cause saturation of the KDEL retrieval system (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Protein sorting by COPII maintains resident leakage rates substantially below the threshold level to render a useful dynamic range to the KDEL retrieval system under normal conditions.
source: Although the data are semi-quantitative, they suggest that protein sorting by COPII maintains resident leakage rates substantially below the threshold level, to render a useful dynamic range to the KDEL retrieval system under normal conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations of GRP94 secretion patterns.

claim: Forward transport of the KDEL receptor substantially exceeds that of KDEL ligands through the combination of receptor concentration and ligand depletion in COPII vesicles.
source: Implicit in this interpretation is that forward transport of the KDEL receptor substantially exceeds that of KDEL ligands, through the combination of receptor concentration (Martínez-Menárguez et al., 1999) and ligand depletion (Figure 4) in COPII vesicles.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: ER residency is stringently imposed in unstressed cells by synergy of the COPII-dependent retention and KDEL-dependent retrieval mechanisms.
source: Generally, we interpret the behavior to indicate that ER residency is stringently imposed in unstressed cells by synergy of the COPII-dependent retention and KDEL-dependent retrieval mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: 4-PBA causes the extracellular secretion of a KDEL-tagged luminal resident in addition to restoring the trafficking of misfolded mutant LDL receptor.
source: In summary, 4-PBA causes the extracellular secretion of a KDEL-tagged luminal resident in addition to restoring the trafficking of misfolded mutant LDL receptor, thereby phenocopying p24 mutant yeast and worms (Elrod-Erickson and Kaiser, 1996; Wen and Greenwald, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 5, and citations to prior literature.

claim: The potency with which 4-PBA analogs restore trafficking of mutant LDL receptor increases in rank order of affinity for COPII protein.
source: Strikingly, the potency with which 4-PBA analogs restore trafficking of mutant LDL receptor increases in rank order of affinity for COPII protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing cell-based assays and fluorescence polarization binding assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: COPII recognition of the ΦC motif mediates ~6 fold concentrative sorting of p24 proteins into vesicles.
source: The results of budding experiments show that COPII recognition of the ΦC motif mediates ~6 fold concentrative sorting of p24 proteins into vesicles, in line with previous measurements of 5–20-fold signal-mediated concentration of cargo and machinery molecules into COPII vesicles (Balch et al., 1994; Malkus et al., 2002; Martínez-Menárguez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: COPII can exclude resident and misfolded proteins by a factor of 4–9-fold.
source: Our data demonstrate that COPII can in addition exclude resident and misfolded proteins by a factor of 4–9-fold.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A modified form of BiP lacking the KDEL retrieval signal is secreted from animal cells 5-fold more slowly than a protein tracer of bulk flow.
source: Comparison with data on BiP suggests that this may be a reasonable measure of the magnitude of the ER retention process: a modified form of BiP lacking the KDEL retrieval signal is secreted from animal cells 5-fold more slowly than a protein tracer of bulk flow (Barlowe and Helenius, 2016; Munro and Pelham, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: By an active sorting mechanism COPII may concentrate cargo and deplete residents, to yield cargo purification of between 25- and 100-fold in a single budding event.
source: Thus, by an active sorting mechanism COPII may concentrate cargo and deplete residents, to yield cargo purification of between 25- and 100-fold in a single budding event.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and comparison with literature values.

claim: Anterograde cargoes are excluded from COPI budding vesicles that mediate retrograde traffic to the ER.
source: The subsequent purification step seems to occur at the intermediate compartment as anterograde cargoes are excluded from COPI budding vesicles that mediate retrograde traffic to the ER (Martínez-Menárguez et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Stringent ER retention requires the efficient packaging of p24 proteins via the B site of the COPII coat.
source: Stringent ER retention requires the efficient packaging of p24 proteins via the B site of the COPII coat.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: When signal-mediated packaging is prevented by B-site mutation, there remains an appreciable (25% of wild-type level) passive uptake into vesicles.
source: When signal-mediated packaging is prevented by B-site mutation, there remains an appreciable (25% of wild-type level) passive uptake into vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only those p24 proteins bound to the polymerized COPII coat can be organized into a luminal array capable of excluding resident protein complexes.
source: However, we suggest that only those p24 proteins bound to the polymerized COPII coat can be organized into a luminal array capable of excluding resident protein complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: The concept of a p24 array that drives resident-protein exclusion implies that coat polymerization and resident exclusion are coupled processes.
source: The concept of a p24 array that drives resident-protein exclusion implies that coat polymerization and resident exclusion are coupled processes.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the proposed model.

claim: Emp24p and Erv25p were identified as suppressors of the essential sec13 gene.
source: First, the principal p24 proteins Emp24p and Erv25p were identified as suppressors of the essential sec13 gene, encoding a component of the COPII outer coat (Elrod-Erickson and Kaiser, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Sec13 lends rigidity to the coat to assist the vesicle budding process.
source: Subsequent analysis indicated that Sec13 lends rigidity to the coat to assist the vesicle budding process (Copic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: An impaired (△Sec13) COPII coat can bud vesicles from p24-depleted membranes, but not from wild-type membranes.
source: Thus, the finding that an impaired (△Sec13) COPII coat can bud vesicles from p24-depleted membranes, but not from wild-type membranes, yielded the surprising insight that p24 proteins mediate against vesicle formation in some manner; that is, the coat must do extra work in a wild-type p24 background (Copic et al., 2012; Elrod-Erickson and Kaiser, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: p24 proteins, by virtue of their asymmetric topology, increase the local membrane-bending energy and oppose curvature induction by the COPII coat.
source: It was proposed that p24 proteins, by virtue of their asymmetric topology (i.e. predominantly luminal mass), increase the local membrane-bending energy and oppose curvature induction by the COPII coat (Copic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a model proposed in prior literature, supported by a citation.

claim: The extra work done by COPII corresponds to force exerted to displace resident complexes from the COPII bud as COPII self-assembly drives together the bound p24 proteins.
source: The results we have presented here suggest the additional or alternative explanation that the extra work is done as COPII self-assembly drives together the bound p24 proteins, and corresponds to force exerted thereby to displace resident complexes from the COPII bud.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: p24 proteins are the most abundant transmembrane constituents of COPII vesicles.
source: They are known to be the most abundant transmembrane constituents of COPII vesicles (Otte et al., 2001), but their stoichiometric relation to COPII protein, their oligomeric structure, and thus the nature of the putative array are all uncertain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ER chaperones form highly dynamic, partially calcium-dependent complexes that are only marginally stable even at the very high macromolecule concentrations that prevail in the ER lumen.
source: These seem to form highly dynamic, partially calcium-dependent complexes that are only marginally stable even at the very high macromolecule concentrations that prevail in the ER lumen (Meunier et al., 2002; Tatu and Helenius, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: 4-PBA is FDA-approved as a prodrug for the treatment of urea cycle disorders.
source: Finally, 4-PBA is FDA-approved as a prodrug for the treatment of urea cycle disorders; it is rapidly metabolized by β-oxidation to phenylacetate, which is conjugated with glutamine in the liver to provide an alternate route for waste nitrogen excretion (Brusilow, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 4-PBA is rapidly metabolized by β-oxidation to phenylacetate.
source: Finally, 4-PBA is FDA-approved as a prodrug for the treatment of urea cycle disorders; it is rapidly metabolized by β-oxidation to phenylacetate, which is conjugated with glutamine in the liver to provide an alternate route for waste nitrogen excretion (Brusilow, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Phenylacetate is conjugated with glutamine in the liver to provide an alternate route for waste nitrogen excretion.
source: Finally, 4-PBA is FDA-approved as a prodrug for the treatment of urea cycle disorders; it is rapidly metabolized by β-oxidation to phenylacetate, which is conjugated with glutamine in the liver to provide an alternate route for waste nitrogen excretion (Brusilow, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: 4-PBA restores trafficking of misfolded proteins and mitigates ER stress in a range of in vitro systems and in animal models of metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: A growing body of evidence demonstrates the distinct property of 4-PBA to restore trafficking of misfolded proteins and to mitigate ER stress in a range of in vitro systems, and in animal models of metabolic and neurodegenerative diseases (Bondulich et al., 2016; Ozcan et al., 2006; Rubenstein et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.
